paper_title: MomentMem: Memorizing Key Moments for Robot Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering visual information that is no longer observable, such as the original location of an object. Existing approaches typically rely on full observation histories, which become redundant over long horizons, or text summaries, which may omit precise visual details. We study visual moment memory, the ability to retain such details from key moments for subsequent manipulation. To support this study, we introduce VMBench, a suite of long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring memory of spatial locations, visual appearances, and their associations. We further propose MomentMem, a hierarchical architecture in which a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes and an executor predicts actions conditioned on the selected memories. This separation enables us to evaluate memory selection alongside closed-loop task success and to study memorizer generalization independently of the executor. On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points. Moreover, we find that the memorizer transfers well to unseen appearances zero-shot. It can also adapt to an unseen task with only a few memory annotations, reaching 43.7% success, close to the 44.3% obtained with full memory supervision. Further experiments show competitive performance on RMBench and improvements in real-robot manipulation. These results highlight the value of retaining sparse visual evidence for memory-dependent manipulation. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MomentMem.

sections.content: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering visual information that is no longer observable, such as the original location of an object. These results highlight the value of retaining sparse visual evidence for memory1 dependent manipulation. Our code is available at https: //github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MomentMem. 1. Introduction Recently, memory has increasingly become key capability of multi-modal models [18, 30, 37, 41] and embodied models [19, 28, 29, 31]. Despite advances in embodied models [4, 12, 21], memory for robot manipulation remains challenging. As shown in Figure 1(a), existing approaches often focus on full observation histories [35] or text descriptions [5, 34]. Full observation histories are complete yet redundant, thus falling short when facing long-horizon tasks [37, 38]. Text captures abstract events, yet can omit visual details, or cannot fully describe certain information (e.g., move the cube back to where it was). To this end, we study visual moment memory for robotic manipulation. It requires models to remember precise visual information at key moment, such as texture patterns, spatial relations, and spatial locations. This type of memory is difficult to preserve in text. As first step, we propose VMBench, benchmark of long-horizon manipulation tasks that require visual moment memory. Its key design principle is to make successful manipulation depend on remembering precise visual information. Different from existing benchmarks [5, 7, 10, 22], our benchmark emphasizes tasks that cannot be well addressed by concise text memory. Specifically, these tasks require remembering exact positions and visual patterns, rather than only object identities or task progress. Concise text summaries may omit these details, as illustrated in Figure 1(b). We organize the tasks around spatial locations, visual appearances, and appearance-location bindings. For example, returning cube to its original position requires remembering exactly where it was, rather than just knowing that it was moved. Across these tasks, the key visual moment is only visible across short period of time and the model has to capture such moments for successful task completion. Together, these tasks provide testbed for studying how robots memorize precise visual information for manipulation tasks. Going further, we consider the modeling of visual moment memory for robot manipulation. Task success alone does not reveal whether failure comes from memory or execution [32]. Beyond overall task performance, we seek to examine two key capabilities: memory selection and action prediction. To this end, we propose MomentMem, hierarchical architecture that separates memory from action prediction. This separation allows us to examine memory selection and action execution independently. As shown in Figure 1(c) (top), VLM memorizer selects keyframes, and then the executor predicts actions. We observe that the key event often spans across several frames that show the same visual cue. We annotate this span as temporal segment. We aim for the memorizer to select keyframe in the segment as early as possible. Also, if it misses an earlier frame, it should still try to capture the later frame in the same segment. During inference, the executor predicts actions from the selected keyframes together with the current observation. Details are provided in Section 4. With our benchmark tasks and hierarchical model, we design metrics and protocols to evaluate end-to-end success rate and the generalization of memory capability, as shown in Figure 1(c). As in most existing benchmarks, we test the models on our benchmark tasks and measure the success rate over closed-loop rollouts. We evaluate how well the memorizer captures the relevant evidence. We also test its transfer to unseen appearances and adaptation to new tasks. As shown in Figure 1(c) (bottom), we vary the visual appearance and directly test the overall model, with the memorizer trained only on the original visual appearances. Besides, we test the overall model for unseen tasks, allowing the memorizer to adapt to new tasks with few memory annotations. In both protocols, we train the executor on target-domain action demonstrations using memories predicted by the memorizer. In other words, our protocols measure the generalization of the memorizer rather than the executor. On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points. In addition, the memorizer transfers zero-shot to unseen appearances. With only few memory annotations, it adapts to an unseen task. The resulting policy reaches 43.7% success, close to 44.3% with full memory supervision. Beyond VMBench, MomentMem remains competitive on RMBench and improves task success in real-robot manipulation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of MomentMem. Our contributions are as follows: We identify visual moment memory as key research problem for robotic manipulation, focusing on remembering transient, precise visual information. We introduce VMBench to evaluate and study this problem in closed-loop manipulation tasks. We also propose MomentMem, hierarchical model that supports separate diagnosis of memory and action prediction. Extensive experiments show that MomentMem exceeds the strongest baseline on our VMBench by 31.7 percentage points. Our analysis demonstrates that the memorizer can transfer to unseen appearance and task. Further, MomentMem performs well on RMBench and real-robot tasks. 2. Related Work 2.1. Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models leverage pretrained vision-language representations to generate robot actions. RT-2 [42] transferred web-scale semantic knowledge to 2 robotic control, while OpenVLA [21] and Octo [13] developed open generalist policies trained on diverse robot data. Recent models, including π0 [3], π0.5 [4], GR00T series [25], GigaBrain series [1416], and Gemini Robotics [12], improve action generation and cross-task generalization. Despite these advances, most VLAs condition on the current observation or short context window. They therefore struggle when relevant evidence has disappeared from view [3, 6, 8, 28]. Our work addresses this limitation by providing VLA models with task-relevant keyframes identified from earlier observations. 2.2. Robotic Manipulation Policies with Memory Some robotic manipulation tasks require evidence from earlier observations, motivating policies that use interaction history [5, 11, 28]. Available information includes the task instruction, visual observations, actions, and proprioceptive states. Existing memory methods differ in how they store and use historical information. Some methods maintain recurrent states, memory banks, or compressed tokens to retain information from long histories [1, 8, 19, 20, 23, 27, 28, 35]. Compressing long histories may discard visual details needed for later actions. Other methods summarize the history with language or use textual plans as memory [5, 31, 34]. Such representations are compact, but concise text summaries may omit task-relevant visual details, such as fine-grained appearances. Another line of work directly selects observations from the visual history [29]. This preserves raw visual evidence, though several methods select with predefined rules or heuristics [6, 22, 39, 40]. Such rules may need adjustment when memory requirements change. Our method learns when to save observations that contain evidence needed for later actions. It uses hierarchical architecture with separate memorizer and executor modules. The most closely related method is EventVLA [38], which predicts keyframes from predicted future actions within single model. Our memorizer instead selects keyframes from visual observations independently of action prediction. 2.3. Robotic Memory Benchmarks Several benchmarks evaluate memory in robotic manipulation. RMBench [5] supports systematic evaluation of memory in robotic imitation learning. MIKASA-Robo [7] and RoboMME [10] evaluate multiple dimensions of memory, while MemoryBench [11] focuses on spatial memory and action recall. Other benchmarks focus on memory in long-horizon tasks, which involve extended trajectories and require precise manipulation [9, 22, 26, 38]. Complementing these benchmarks, VMBench focuses on visual moment memory: recalling precise visual evidence that is visible only for short period of time. We study memorizer transfer using visual OOD variants and few-shot adaptation on held-out task. 3. VMBench: Evaluating Visual Moment

sections.title: Memory
sections.content: We introduce VMBench that necessitates visual moment memory during robot manipulation. It contains nine closedloop manipulation tasks, requiring the model to recall precise visual details which text summaries are hard to describe. This evidence is briefly presented by the environment or revealed through interaction. In some tasks, the environment presents the evidence before execution. In others, the robot must act to reveal it, such as opening drawers or scanning with detector. These settings test memory during both observation and active manipulation. Appendix describes the key evidence in each task, and appendix provides complete task instructions for all tasks in VMBench. 3.1. Types of Visual Evidence We categorize the tasks by their visual information requirements. Table 1 provides an overview. Spatial locations. These tasks require recalling precise spatial locations. The policy must retain spatial reference for later movement or search. For example, Flash Beacon requires the robot to place the cube where the beacon appeared. Visual appearance. These tasks require retaining detailed visual patterns. The policy must compare appearances observed at different times, even when object categories alone cannot distinguish them. For example, Scroll Discovery requires the robot to retract scrolls, remembering the revealed patterns, and then stack the two scrolls with matching patterns after they roll back up. Appearance-location bindings. These tasks require retaining associations between appearances and locations. Remembering the appearances or locations separately is insufficient; the policy must preserve their correspondence. For example, the robot scans the minefield with detector. The detector briefly changes color at each target location. After scanning, the robot places colored blocks at these locations, so it must remember where each color appeared. in Mine Sweeper, 3.2. Demonstrations and Memory Annotations We collect 100 successful demonstrations per task. Each demonstration contains annotated key segments. We obtain these segments from simulator events and task state. Each segment marks when one piece of task-relevant evidence is visible. It allows multiple valid frames rather than prescribing single representative. The annotations support both training and evaluation of keyframe selection. VMBench is built on SAPIEN [36] and ManiSkill3 [17, 24, 33]. We collect demonstrations using Franka Panda manipulator and scripted closed-loop experts. Trajectories record RGB images from overview and wrist cameras at 224 224 resolution, with control 3 Table 1. Overview of the tasks in VMBench. Appendix details data collection, randomization, and annotation. 3.3. Visual OOD Setting To test memory transfer across visual appearances, we provide visual out-of-distribution (OOD) variant of each task. We change room and table appearance, lighting, and distractors outside the manipulation area. Task mechanics, memory events, and success conditions remain unchanged. This setting tests whether memorizer trained on standard appearances can directly generate useful memories under unseen appearances. The executor is trained on target-domain action demonstrations. 3.4. Memory Evaluation We evaluate complete policies by closed-loop task success. For methods that explicitly select keyframes, the interval annotations also support separate evaluation of memory selection. We replay recorded demonstrations, using each models previous selections as its memory context. Segment hit rate measures the fraction of intervals with at least one selected frame. Segment accuracy requires exactly one selection per interval. Non-keyframe accuracy measures the fraction of demonstrations with no selections outside the annotated intervals. These metrics distinguish missed evidence, duplicate selections, and selections outside the intervals. Appendix gives the details and results. 4. MomentMem 4.1. Overview As shown in Figure 2, MomentMem uses hierarchical architecture that decouples memory from action execution. VLM memorizer processes streaming visual observations and selects keyframes. VLA executor uses these keyframes and the current observation to predict actions. This design addresses two challenges of visual moment memory. We use sparse keyframes as the interface between memory and execution. Keyframes preserve raw images to retain visual details needed for later actions. The memorizer uses recent observations and existing memory to decide when to save frame. It captures transient evidence while avoiding duplicate storage. Online interaction. At time t, the robot receives an observation ot, proprioceptive state st, and task instruction l. The memorizer πM decides whether to store the current frame using the existing memory Mt1, buffer Bt of recent subsampled observations including ot, and the instruction. The executor πE predicts an action chunk At from the updated memory Mt and the current input: pt = πM (Yes Mt1, Bt, l), Mt = Mt1 {ot : pt > 0.5}, At πE( Mt, ot, st, l). (1) The executor receives the selected keyframes in temporal order rather than the full observation history. Training pipeline. We first train the memorizer with key segment annotations. We then freeze it to generate memories for action demonstrations. The executor takes the memorized keyframes as input and learns to predict the demonstration actions. The details are elaborated in the following subsections. 4.2. The Memorizer of MomentMem We fine-tune VLM to output Yes or No given the context in Equation 1, indicating whether to store the current frame. Training must allow multiple valid frames for each event and account for how earlier selections affect the current decision. Segment-level supervision. Visual evidence often remains visible across several frames. Labeling only one fixed frame as correct would penalize other valid selections. Our supervision instead allows different representatives of the same evidence across training epochs. For each piece of visual evidence, we annotate an interval Sj = [uj, vj] during which it is visible. Each epoch, we select one representative frame, called an anchor, from each interval. The memorizer is trained to identify the anchors and reject others. We generate intervals automatically in simulation, and annotate them manually for real-world experiments. Anchor sampling. At the start of each epoch, we sample one anchor cj per interval. Under teacher-forced history, the anchor receives positive label and enters memory. Earlier frames in the same interval are excluded from the loss but remain in the recent observation context. Later frames and frames outside all intervals receive negative labels. Resampling across epochs teaches the model to select different valid representatives of the same event. The memorizer is encouraged to capture visual evidence when it appears. If it misses an opportunity, it can select later valid frame. We use focal loss to address the imbalance between positive and negative samples. Scheduled sampling. Whether frame should be stored depends on what is already in memory. The same evidence may need to be saved after missed selection, but becomes redundant once representative is stored. Missed or extra selections during execution therefore change later inputs and decisions. Training only with teacher-forced histories does not expose the memorizer to these cases. We use sequence-level scheduled sampling to train with histories that include model predictions. At the start of each epoch, the current model replays the training trajectories. We then mix teacher decisions and model predictions to construct memory histories. The probability of using model predictions increases during training. Supervision follows the history provided: after missed anchor, later valid frames in the same interval remain positive. Once representative is stored, subsequent frames become negative. Appendix details label construction. 4.3. The Executor of MomentMem The executor learns to act on the memories that the memorizer actually provides. We therefore freeze the trained memorizer and replay action demonstrations in temporal order. Its selections form the memory context for executor training. The memorizer may select frames at different times, miss relevant evidence, or store extra frames. Training with these predicted memories exposes the executor to the memorizers outputs rather than only to frames sampled from annotated intervals. For training sample at time t, the executor receives predicted keyframes from before t, the current observation ot, the state st, and the instruction l. We supervise it with the demonstration action chunk using the original learning objective of the action policy. This interface supports separate adaptation of memory and execution. In the visual OOD experiments, we reuse the memorizer directly. For new task, we first adapt it with few memory annotations. In both settings, the executor is trained on target-domain action demonstrations. So, this hierarchical design allows us to evaluate the two modules separately. 5. Experiments and Results We first evaluate overall task success on VMBench. We then test the memorizers transfer to unseen appearances and adaptation to new task. We find that MomentMem improves closed-loop success on tasks that require visual moment memory. The memorizer also generalizes to unseen appearance and task to some extent. Beyond VMBench, we test MomentMem on RMBench and real-robot tasks. The results suggest that MomentMem is broadly applicable to memory-dependent manipulation. 5.1. Experimental Setup Implementation and Evaluation. We initialize the memorizer from Qwen3-VL-4B and the executor from π0.5. We use 100 demonstrations per task provided by 5 Figure 2. Overview of MomentMem. (a) The memorizer uses recent observations and existing memory to decide whether to store the current frame. The executor predicts actions from the updated memory and current input. (b) Each epoch, we sample an anchor from each key segment. Under teacher-forced history, the anchor is positive. Earlier frames in the segment remain in the observation context but are excluded from the loss. Later frames are negative because the event has been stored. VMBench and jointly train all nine tasks. We first train the memorizer with annotated key segments and then freeze it. We use its predicted keyframes to train the executor on action demonstrations. At test time, the executor receives online-selected keyframes, the current observation, the robot state, and the task instruction. Appendix provides the detailed training configuration. Baselines. We compare MomentMem against π0.5 [4] and three memory-augmented policies. Mem-0 [5] uses explicit memory and high-level planning to guide action execution. NativeMEM [35] compresses past observations into memory tokens. EventVLA [38] learns sparse visual evidence memory jointly with action prediction. All methods use the same demonstrations and joint training as MomentMem. Each task is evaluated on 100 rollouts with unseen initial configurations. 5.2. MomentMem Improves Success on Visual

sections.title: Moment Memory Tasks
sections.content: MomentMem substantially improves closed-loop success. As shown in Table 2, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, 31.7% above the strongest baseline. It performs best on five tasks and ties for best on one more. The largest gains occur on Placement Imitation, Mine Sweeper, and Seal Checking, which require retaining precise visual evidence after it disappears from view. Memory-free execution struggles on these tasks. π0.5 reaches only 7.0% average success, and scores 0% on four of the nine tasks. On Mine Sweeper, we observe that π0.5 often places block inside the candidate region, but not at the location specified by the earlier visual cue. This suggests that learning how to pick and place block is not enough. The policy must also remember where to place it. Texture matching remains difficult for the executor. MomentMem gains most on tasks requiring appearance location bindings. In contrast, MomentMem does not outperform the strongest baseline on the Appearance tasks. To understand this, we run diagnosis on Hidden Pattern. Linear probes of the executors final-layer features predict what the texture is with 99% accuracy, but predict the matching box with only 40% accuracy, just slightly higher than the 33% level of random guessing. The features retain information about each texture, but do not capture well which textures match. Appendix gives the setup and additional readouts. These results suggest that the executor struggles to match textures across memory images, even when the relevant evidence is available. 5.3. Memory Selection Transfers to Unseen Visual

As shown in Table 4, MomentMem reaches 69.8% average success, 1.9 percentage points above EventVLA at 67.9%. It obtains the best result on six of the nine tasks, including 61% gain over the strongest baseline on Observe and Pick Up. The architecture thus remains effective on memory tasks beyond VMBench. MomentMem also improves task success on real robot. We evaluate MomentMem on Franka Panda robot using real-world counterparts of Placement Imitation and Explore Cube, as illustrated in Figure 4. We collect 51 and 54 demonstrations respectively, and manually annotate their key segments. As shown in Table 5, MomentMem completes 17 more episodes than π0.5 and 15 more than EventVLA across the 60 trials. The larger gain occurs on Placement Imitation, where the robot must remember the demonstrated location after the cube is moved away. 5.6. We replace each annotated segment with single positive frame, following the point annotation used by prior work. As shown in Table 6, this change reduces average success by 43.0 percentage points. Point supervision treats neighboring frames as negatives simply because they are not the selected anchor frame. However, nearby frames may show the same evidence. Labeling them as negative penalizes valid selections. Segment supervision avoids this problem. Scheduled sampling improves success on multi-event tasks. Discussion on Memory Capability The memorizer can capture most key segments. Our method adopts hierarchical architecture. This design lets us evaluate memory selection separately from execution. We use the simulator to verify whether the memorizer selects frame in the key moment segment. On the validation set, it captures 95.8% of key segments, while it avoids selecting frame outside the key moment segment in 84.4% of demonstrations. These results validate the training of our memorizer and show how memory selection can be evaluated directly. Appendix gives the full setup and per-task results. Our memorizer works better than stronger frozen VLM. Our memorizer is trained with the key segment annotations from humans or the simulator. natural question is whether stronger VLM can select keyframes without post-training, as in BPP [29]. To test this hypothesis, we follow BPP and exploit frozen GPT-6-Astra to identify when key event occurs. However, querying such VLM is costly, and thus we do not run the closed-loop evaluation. Instead, we compare the keyframe selection on the same validation split using the same memory metrics. It turns out that GPT-6-Astra captures only 69.5% of key segments. The results demonstrate that our memorizer works clearly better than the stronger frozen VLM, which we attribute to memory training and annotations. Therefore, general visual understanding is not strong enough for memory capability and memory modeling deserves more attention from the community. Appendix provides the full setup and per-task results. 6. Conclusion We study visual moment memory, which requires robots to retain precise visual details for later execution. We introduce VMBench, whose tasks require remembering briefly visible locations, appearances, and their associations. We propose MomentMem, which decouples memory from execution: VLM memorizer stores sparse keyframes as raw images, and an executor predicts actions from them. MomentMem improves task success on VMBench and real robot, and remains competitive on RMBench. Its memorizer transfers zero-shot to unseen appearances and adapts to held-out task with few memory annotations. Future work can investigate whether broader memory training enables transfer to new tasks without memory annotations. Limitations. MomentMem runs VLM memorizer, which adds inference cost compared with single-model policy. On RMBench, MomentMem improves average success by 1.9 percentage points over the strongest evaluated baseline, but gains vary across tasks. The executor still struggles to use retained texture information for target selection, even when the relevant evidence is available (Appendix F.1). VMBench also uses single embodiment and fixed camera configuration, so the effect of viewpoint changes remains untested.

Dataset Construction C.1. Simulation and Demonstration Collection We construct VMBench in ManiSkill3 with SAPIEN physics, using Panda manipulator, an overview camera, and wrist camera. The data-generation pipeline records both RGB streams at 224224 resolution and control frequency of 20 Hz. Each task implements scripted, closed-loop expert that computes actions from the simulator state and executes them through the robot controller. Demonstrations therefore contain the actions actually applied to the environment and the resulting observations. Each rollout starts from seeded initialization, with the scene rebuilt at reset. Task-specific randomization varies object positions, target locations, and the associations between visual cues and their required responses. For example, Hidden Pattern samples distinct patterns and assigns them to boxes. Drawer Match and Scroll Discovery randomize the matching patterns. Placement Imitation, Mine Sweeper, and Seal Checking randomize colorlocation associations. Color pairs are sampled without replacement from palette of eight colors, excluding pairs that are too similar under the implemented color-distance criterion. Spatial sampling also enforces task-specific separation and reachability constraints. These variations produce different memory contents while retaining the same task instruction. The expert rolls out until success, failure, termination, or the step limit. Only successful episodes are retained. Failed attempts are discarded, and generation continues with new seeds. For tasks that expose separate evaluation-success flag, retained demonstration must satisfy that flag as well as the experts success condition. Our main experiment uses 100 demonstrations per task, giving 900 demonstrations across the nine tasks. C.2. Automatic Memory Annotations Each environment records the key segments during which task-relevant evidence is available, using simulator events and task state. Each segment is stored as an inclusive pair of frame indices [uj, vj] at the original recording rate. The metadata also records the event identity, the information to retain, and the corresponding timestamps. These segments mark valid ranges rather than fixed representative frames. Each demonstration has one to three annotated segments, as summarized in Table 7. For Seal Checking, each segment ends before the revealed color becomes too faint to identify. Privileged event metadata supplies supervision for memory selection and is not included in the memorizers or executors observation input. C.3. Observation and Action Alignment Raw trajectories are saved in HDF5, with accompanying JSON metadata containing the episode seed, task instruction, phase intervals, and memory annotations. rollout with actions contains observations from o0 through oT . Conversion creates training records, pairing each action at with its preceding observation ot and timestamp. The terminal observation is not assigned an additional action. Both camera streams and the key segment boundaries use this frame indexing. Hidden Pattern, Spring Compression, and Placement Imitation begin with an observation phase in which the environment presents visual demonstration without requesting policy actions. These observations remain available for memory selection. For MomentMem, the recorded stationary actions during these observation phases are excluded from action supervision, and the executor is trained only on the execution phase. The remaining tasks require robot actions to acquire the evidence, so their recorded actions remain eligible for supervision throughout the trajectory. Our EventVLA implementation instead retains supervision on these stationary actions, because its keyframe predictions are derived from action hidden states. It therefore learns these actions even though the environment does not request them during observation. C.4. Training-Data Conversion We convert the recordings into LeRobot-format datasets with per-episode videos, tabular stateaction records, task metadata, and separate file of key-segment annotations. The converter checks camera streams, temporal alignment, and segment bounds, and rejects missing or malformed segments. It reconstructs the controllers commanded targets from recorded simulator states to express end-effector actions in the overview-camera coordinate system. For the executor used in this paper, actions comprise relative end-effector translation, relative rotation represented in Rot6D, and gripper command. Dataset conversion preserves the annotated key segments. Anchor sampling is performed during training, as described in Section 4. C.5. Visual OOD Data Visual OOD environments use the same task implementations and expert procedures, with altered room and table appearance, lighting, and additional background or tabletop distractors outside the manipulation area. Appearance randomization uses S3 separate seed-derived random-number stream, preserving the task randomization for given seed. Task mechanics, memory events, and success conditions are shared with the standard setting, and OOD trajectories pass through the same recording and conversion pipeline. In the appearance-transfer experiment, target-domain executor training uses keyframes predicted by the transferred memorizer rather than the simulators target-domain memory annotations. D. The executor receives current overview and wrist images, while its keyframe stack contains only overview images. The memorizer receives neither privileged memory instructions nor absolute historical frame indices. VMBench operates at 20 Hz, and the memorizer samples observations at 5 Hz. We study Hidden Pattern, Flash Beacon, and Seal Checking as examples of the Appearance, Spatial, and Spatial & Appearance categories, respectively. We compare MomentMem with EventVLA, the baseline with the highest average success in the standard setting. We examine whether relevant evidence is retained, whether it influences subsequent actions, and whether the required physical operations are completed. We also evaluate whether keyframe selection remains effective under visual appearance changes. All analyses use the final checkpoints on ten fixed test scenes per task, without further training. F.1. Counterfactual Keyframe Content If stored cue guides the robots choice, changing the cue should change which target it chooses. Protocol. We use the same scene seeds for both methods. Each scene is assigned original and counterfactual conditions. The counterfactual branch runs only when the intervention point is reached. It then edits the cue content in eligible keyframes selected by the method itself. Scenes without an intervention point or an eligible selected frame remain in the counts. For Seal Checking, we exchange the two colors of the seal in the stored keyframes. BPP-Style Selection with Frozen VLM Following BPP, we prompt frozen VLM, GPT-6-Astra, to decide whether each frame shows key event. hand-written prompt specifies the key events of each task. We use the overview camera as input, since the task-relevant information is visible in it. The original BPP queries the VLM at 1 Hz, which can miss key segments shorter than one second. We therefore query at 2 Hz, and each query contains the current frame and the frame 0.5 earlier. keyframe is marked at each transition from no to yes. Because of the cost of querying the VLM, we do not run closed-loop evaluation. Since the selected keyframes directly determine the executors input, we instead evaluate keyframe selection on the same validation split and with the same metrics as Table 10. As shown in Table 17, the frozen VLM captures 69.5% of key segments, compared with 95.8% for MomentMem. It fails on Spring Compression and Placement Imitation and is weak on Scroll Discovery. BPP marks about 4.2% of the non-key frames it evaluates as keyframes, compared with 0.14% for MomentMem. Over long demonstration, BPP therefore selects more false keyframes than true key events. We identify two causes. First, each query sees only two images. Spring Compression and Placement Imitation require the moment when an object reaches its farthest position, but two frames cannot show whether it has started to return. MomentMem mitigates both problems in training. Anchor sampling treats any frame in key segment as valid choice, so the memorizer can still select later frame if it misses an earlier one.
